The Months Before a Baby Arrives

For the months before a baby comes, when advice arrives faster than answers. It gets your questions written down for short appointments, settles who is told what, packs the bag early, and checks what your leave and pay actually are.

Pregnancy · Parenting · Body · Life Transitions · 9 items · once a week

The checklist

  • Write your questions down as they occur to you — appointments are short and memory is worse than you think.
  • Decide together who gets told what, and when — one agreed answer saves repeating yourself all month.
  • Say the frightening thought out loud to one person — unspoken fear gets very loud at night.
  • Pack the bag four weeks before you think you need to — early is calm and late is frantic.
  • Work out what the first two weeks at home need — meals, a sleeping plan, who comes and when.
  • Ask what your leave and pay actually are, in writing — assumptions here turn out expensive.
  • Keep one thing that is entirely yours — a baby takes the calendar, not the whole person.
  • Tell your midwife or doctor about low mood now — the weeks before count, not only the weeks after.
  • Let the birth plan be a preference, not a promise — the day rarely reads the document.

Use this checklist Free account: tick items off and keep each day's record.

How to use it

Run through it once a week, honestly and without scoring yourself. A checklist is a way of noticing, not a test: an item you cannot tick is information about the day, not a verdict on you. Over a few weeks the pattern of what gets ticked and what does not says more than any single pass.

With a free Theraglee account the checklist remembers each pass, so you can look back. Without one, you can still read it here and keep your own copy.
